extracted.intended_audience: YALSA Printz Award committee members, YALSA staff, and publishers/authors seeking eligibility/nomination guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Official policies and procedures for the Michael L. Printz Award: committee composition, eligibility and nomination rules, evaluation criteria for selecting the year's best young adult book (defined by literary merit), and voting/balloting processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / Primary purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The Michael L. Printz Award recognizes the best titles in young adult literature in a given calendar year. The Committee is to select from the previous year's publications the best young adult book ("best" being defined solely in terms of literary merit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The award will: recognize the best in the field of materials for young adults; promote books published for young adults; inspire readership; give recognition to the genre; position YALSA as an authority in evaluating and selecting materials for teen library collections. The ALA press release announcing the winner should stipulate why the title has been chosen for its literary excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: What quality is not (exclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: POPULARITY is not the criterion for this award. Nor is MESSAGE. CONTROVERSY is not something to avoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The award hopes for a wide audience among readers 12–18 but explicitly excludes popularity and message as criteria; controversial books are acceptable and may be desirable ('we want a book that readers will talk about').

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Librarianship focuses on individuals, in all their diversity, and that focus is a fundamental value of YALSA. Diversity is, thus, honored in the Association and in the collections and services that libraries provide to young adults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversity should be respected as part of evaluation and selection — works reflecting diverse individuals and experiences are within the Award's values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility and avoidance of rigid criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria change with time. Therefore, flexibility and an avoidance of the too-rigid are essential components of these criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of 'too-rigid criteria' to avoid include demanding "a realistic hope," avoiding complicated plot, or requiring strict originality — many great books defy such fixed rules (examples: Robert Cormier's Chocolate War; Louis Sachar's Holes). Evaluators should adapt criteria to the book and allow varying weight for different qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligible forms and formats
rubrics_metrics.description: The award-winning book may be fiction, nonfiction, poetry or an anthology. All forms of writing—fiction, nonfiction, poetry, art, and any combination of these, including anthologies—are eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations and design are also explicitly recognized criteria (see separate entries). The award may be given posthumously and works of joint authorship or editorship are eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility — publication date
rubrics_metrics.description: Books must have been published between January 1 and December 31 of the year preceding announcement of the award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chair is responsible for verifying the eligibility of all nominated titles. If no title is deemed sufficiently meritorious, no award will be given that year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility — intended audience / designation
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible, a title must have been designated by its publisher as being either a young adult book or one published for the age range that YALSA defines as 'young adult,' i.e., 12 through 18. Adult books are not eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles must be designated by the publisher as YA (12–18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility — previously published foreign works
rubrics_metrics.description: Books previously published in another country are eligible (presuming an American edition has been published during the period of eligibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign works are eligible only if an American edition was published within the eligible year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ineligible until US print/distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles that are self-published, published only in eBook format, and/or published from a publisher outside of the US will not be considered eligible until the first year the book is available in print or distributed through a US publishing house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-published, ebook-only, or non-US-publisher titles must wait until a US print/distribution edition year to be eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested evaluative dimensions (general list)
rubrics_metrics.description: The following criteria are only suggested guidelines and should in no way be considered as absolutes. Depending on the book, one or more of these criteria will apply: Story; Voice; Style; Setting; Accuracy; Characters; Theme; Illustrations; Design (including format, organization, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each book the questions and answers will be different, and the weight of the various criteria will be different. These are suggested axes of literary excellence rather than fixed subcriteria; apply flexibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Story
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is a suggested guideline for judging a title's literary excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider plot, structure, pacing, and how the narrative arc contributes to literary merit; recognize that complex or nontraditional plots can be strengths (see flexibility guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Voice is a suggested guideline for judging a title's literary excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess narrative perspective, authorial voice, and how distinctive or authentic the voice is for the work and intended readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Style
rubrics_metrics.description: Style is a suggested guideline for judging a title's literary excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate language use, sentencecraft, tone, and stylistic choices that contribute to literary quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting is a suggested guideline for judging a title's literary excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how place/time/environment are rendered and how they support theme, character, and story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy is a suggested guideline for judging a title's literary excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate factual correctness where relevant (particularly for nonfiction) and authenticity of detail where accuracy contributes to credibility and merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters is a suggested guideline for judging a title's literary excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess characterization, development, complexity, and how characters drive or embody the work's literary qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Theme is a suggested guideline for judging a title's literary excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate thematic depth, complexity, and how themes are handled (note: 'message' as popularity/advocacy is not itself a criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations are a suggested guideline for judging a title's literary excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the quality and appropriateness of artwork, its contribution to meaning and reading experience, and integration with text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion — Design (format, organization, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design (including format, organization, etc.) is a suggested guideline for judging a title's literary excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider book design, layout, typography, organization and how these elements support readability and literary effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominations — process and required information
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee members may nominate an unlimited number of titles. Each nomination must be made in writing on an official nomination form and should include: author, title, publisher, price, ISBN, and an annotation specifying those qualities that justify the title for consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nominations from committee members need no second. Field suggestions must be submitted on the official suggestion form and must be seconded by a committee member (if no second within 30 days, the title is dropped). Publishers/authors/editors may not suggest or nominate their own titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: All nominated titles must be kept confidential; there will be no announcements of nominated titles. All committee meetings and discussions, including electronic discussions, are closed to YALSA membership and the general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain strict confidentiality of nominations and deliberations to protect the integrity of the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee membership responsibilities and ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Members are required to attend all committee meetings and read widely from books eligible for nomination. All committee members must comply with YALSA's Policies, including Social Media Policy, Ethical Behavior Policy for Volunteers, and the Award Committees Conflict of Interest Policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members serve 12-month terms (Feb 1–Jan 31). Members who have completed one full term on any YALSA award committee may not be appointed to the same or another YALSA award committee for two years from the conclusion of their term (exceptions possible). The chair is a voting member, presides over meetings, must serve as list owner of the committee electronic discussion list, and may request an administrative assistant (non-voting). The Booklist consultant may participate fully in discussion but may not vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calendar / meeting schedule obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: General calendar: May–June appointment of members; December virtual training; Feb 1 committee begins work; By May 15 chair sends list of nominated titles; June ALA Annual Conference three closed sessions; Sept 15 second list; Dec 1 final date for field nominations; Dec 15 final date for member nominations; Jan Midwinter three closed sessions to select winner and honors; June Annual Conference Printz Awards Program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chair develops detailed timeline; members must plan to attend specified closed sessions at Annual and Midwinter meetings; training is provided in December.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting procedures and scoring for winner selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Following discussion, balloting will begin. Paper ballots used; on each ballot each member votes for top three choices: first = 5 points, second = 3 points, third = 1 point. Members must be present to vote; proxies not accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Straw votes may be used at chair's discretion to guide discussion. To win, a title must receive five first-place votes and must also receive at least five more points than the second-place title. If no title meets these criteria, any title receiving no votes is removed and discussion continues, followed by another ballot; balloting continues until a winner is declared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor book selection procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: All nominated titles are eligible for honor book consideration. Following selection of a winner, a straw vote is conducted; any title receiving no votes is removed from consideration. A formal, weighted ballot will follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on ballot results, the committee will decide if it wishes to name honor books and, if so, how many (up to four).

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotations and press release responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The committee is responsible for writing a press release and annotations for the winning title and honor books. Both must include discussion of the literary merits of the titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The annotations and press release must be written prior to the Monday awards press conference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactions with publishers / ethical contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ethical Behavior Policy for Volunteers and the Award Committees Conflict of Interest Policy outline appropriate interactions between committee members and publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chair and/or administrative assistant are responsible for contact with publishers. Committee members must not solicit publishers for free personal copies of books. If members receive, or are offered, unsolicited copies of books from publishers, they may accept the titles. Committee members must not solicit publishers for favors or invitations; if such are received, members should use their judgment in accepting, understanding acceptance does not influence selections.
